How to track weight and body measurements consistently

Numbers only help if they are collected the same way each time. These practical habits make your records easier to trust.

Educational estimates only. Results are not medical advice, a diagnosis, or a treatment plan. Talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your health. Read the full medical disclaimer.

Measure under similar conditions

Body weight naturally moves through the day with food, drink and fluid. Pick a consistent time, for example in the morning, and similar clothing. Do the same for tape measurements, and keep the tape snug but not tight.

Use the same landmarks

For your waist, NICE guidance suggests measuring halfway between the bottom of your ribs and the top of your hips, after breathing out normally. Decide where you will measure hips and chest and repeat the same spots. A mirror or a helper can make it easier to keep the tape level.

Look at trends, not single days

One reading can jump up or down for reasons unrelated to long-term change. Compare readings several weeks apart. The weight progress calculator shows total and average weekly change between two dates, and the measurement tracker charts your records over time.

Keep your records safe

The tracker stores records only in your browser on your device and does not upload them. Clearing your browser data can erase them, so use the Export CSV button now and then to keep a backup copy.

Keep it in perspective

Measurements are a tool, not a verdict. If tracking makes you anxious, or you are thinking about restrictive eating, take a break and talk with a healthcare professional.

Sources and further reading

  • NICE guideline NG246: Identifying and assessing overweight, obesity and central adiposity
